messages.subject: How to get p-values out of MARK? (RMark package)
messages.subject_clean: How to get p-values out of MARK? (RMark package)
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to fit CJS models using MARK, called from R using the RMark package. This is the output I get:

Output summary for CJS model
Name : Phi(~surv_est)p(~1)

Npar :  3
-2lnL:  6711.534
AICc :  6717.537

Beta
                 estimate        se       lcl       ucl
Phi:(Intercept) -2.203400 0.3040294 -2.799297 -1.607502
Phi:surv_est     4.494413 0.8343975  2.858994  6.129832
p:(Intercept)   -1.332056 0.0756035 -1.480239 -1.183874

[... etc..]

... but I would like to see the parameters' p-values as well (not only the estimate and confidence intervals), along with those *** markings which make it easy to see right away, as it is in summaries of all other models in R. Do you have any clue how to force RMark to report summary in this format? I tried various options of ?summary.mark but with no success.

Thanks and best regards!

Tomas

messages.subject: Re: How to get p-values out of MARK? (RMark package)
messages.subject_clean: How to get p-values out of MARK? (RMark package)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

just one question: why do you need p-values for a CJS?

CJS are capture-recapture model, so you will have estimates of survival and detection, AIC associated to the model, and all convergence information, but no p-values are expected in the results of one model.
The only thing you need is given in the summary of RMark: if you want to see if betas are different from zero, just look at the CI.
I suggest you to think about when and why p-values are used.
BTW, there is a forum devoted to RMark and you can find it here: phidot forum - RMARK subtopic <http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewforum.php?f=21&sid=66dfb342b8c53d807ebe92feb60711f3> or in the MARK Book.

Best wishes,

Guillaume

messages.subject: Re: How to get p-values out of MARK? (RMark package)
messages.subject_clean: How to get p-values out of MARK? (RMark package)
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tomas,

My question was about the need of p-values in Capture-recapture framework.
The use of p-values should be motivated by hypothesis testing and biological relevance. Computing p-value to have p-value is useless.

In the present case (CMR), model selection and multi-model inference mostly rely information criterion (AIC/BIC/DIC) rather than p-values (McCrea & Morgan 2014 Analysis of capture-recapture data. CRC Press). The model selection retained the effect based on the likehood of the model corrected for the number of parameters . Then, you have your best model and all effects. Thus, no need of p-values (Mark Book - Chap 4, Lebreton et al 1992 Ecological Monographs, 62, 67-118, Burnham & Anderson 2002 Model selection and multimodel inference: a practical information-theoretic approach Springer). When dealing with temporal or individual covariates, you can ask whether or not the inclusion of such a covariate is improving your model. To do so, you can use the analyse of deviance (AnoDev, see Grosbois et al 2008 Biological Review, 83, 357-399, Lebreton et al 2012 Biometrics, 68, 494-503, Frederiksen et al 2014 Journal of Applied Ecology, 51, 71-81).

>From your example (a simple CJS), we can see that the detection probability on the biological scale was 0.20, obviously different from 0. So, why do you need a p-value to assess the magnitude of the detection rate being higher than 0?

If you want to rank several effects found in the same model (whether this question is biologically relevant), you might just look at their estimates and 95%CI, and say that one is higher than the other one. If you really need p-values, you can make a test by comparing distribution of both estimates (normal distribution with a mean [point estimate] and variance [es^2])

Sorry about the forum. it is usually on. This is a very active forum but it seems that there is some maintenance now. You can try to contact Jeffrey Laake <http://www.afsc.noaa.gov/nmml/personnel/nmmlprofile.php?name=Jeff.Laake> who writes the package RMark and ask him your question.

Regards,

Guillaume

messages.subject: Stable state calculation in JAGS
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to calculate a stable state distribution (similar to a stable age distribution) based on a transition matrix in JAGS. Does anyone know if this is possible?  As far as I can tell, there are no functions in JAGS for deriving eigen vectors from a transition matrix that would facilitate matrix decomposition to solve for the stable state distribution. Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks
Jared

messages.subject: RE: Stable state calculation in JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jared,

I don't know whether that will help but I thought I wanted to send the word out about an exciting new BUGS software: NIMBLE (see http://r-nimble.org/).

This is an R-based, general model fitting software that has adopted the BUGS model-definition language. However, it disconnects model specification in that language (which has so far only been used in Bayesian software, i.e., WB, OB and JAGS) and model fitting: there is a variety of Bayesian and non-Bayesian algorithms available.

They extend the use of the BUGS language and so perhaps it is possible to use R matrix functions inside of a model definition in the BUGS language ?

Kind regards  -  Marc

messages.subject_clean: AW: Stable state calculation in JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jared,

In addition to what Marc has recommended, there are two other options. One possibility is to multiply an arbitraty population vector several times (e.g. 100) with the transition matrix. The population vector then converges to a stable stage distribution. A further option is to do the calculation outside JAGS (using the eigen function in R), analog to the calculation of derived parameters.

With kind regards

Michael
